stories.title: The Baker of Small Loaves
stories.setting: Cairo, early 1200s, a famine year when the Nile failed to rise
stories.reader_note: For anyone who has looked into the bottom of the jar and wondered how it could possibly stretch to the end of the month.

ps: In the year the river forgot to rise, the criers of Cairo came up from the Nilometer on Rawda island with the mark of the water, and for the first time in living memory their voices were low. Every summer of his life, Yunus the baker had heard those voices climb with the flood: fourteen cubits, fifteen, sixteen, and then drums, and the cutting of the canal, and boys leaping into brown water with their clothes on. This year the number stopped short, like a sentence nobody wanted to finish. The men in the flour market did their sums in silence. A river that does not rise is a field that will not drink, and a field that will not drink is bread that will not be.

Yunus ibn Dawud kept an oven in a lane off the saddlers’ market, near the southern gate. It was not a famous oven. It had baked no bread for princes and held no secrets except one: a lump of old dough his father had kept alive for forty years and Yunus for twenty more, the sour mother from which every batch was born. Each night he folded a fistful of the day’s dough back into the jar, and each dawn it had grown in the dark, quietly, the way faithful things grow. He had a wife, Safiyya, a son of nine called Dawud, a daughter of six called Ruqayya, and a trade that put him elbow deep in other people’s hunger.

The famine did not arrive like a storm. It leaked in, like water under a door. First the price of wheat doubled, and people joked about it. Then it doubled again, and they stopped. Barley appeared in loaves that had been proud of their whiteness. The villages upstream began to empty, and thin families drifted to the city gates with cooking pots and nothing to put in them. By winter, the saddlers’ lane had learned a new quiet: the quiet of streets where nobody is selling anything sweet, and the children have stopped shouting because shouting spends strength.

Cairo in a good year is a city you can smell before you can see: frying oil, cumin, dung smoke, river mud, sugar. That winter the smells went out one by one, like lamps. What remained was dust, and the cold ash odour of ovens that had gone dark. Of the fourteen bakers between the two markets, five had shut their doors by the month of Rajab. Their flour had run out, or their courage had. Yunus stayed lit. He told himself it was stubbornness. It was, at first.

Safiyya ran the house the way a pilot runs a boat through rocks, by exact knowledge and no sentiment. She knew the weight of a week in lentils, the price of a winter in oil, and precisely how many cupped handfuls of flour stood between her children and the door of the unthinkable. She had sold one of her dowry bracelets in autumn, quietly, and told no one, and the coins had gone into the flour bin one measure at a time. She was not hard. She was accurate, and in a famine, accuracy is a kind of love.

Yunus had been a boy in the last great dearth, thirty years before. He remembered almost none of it, except this: some mornings, in the worst of it, there had been barley bread on the doorstep. Round rough loaves, still warm, left before the dawn prayer by someone who never once let himself be seen. His father searched for the giver for years and never found him. He would say, to the end of his life, with wonder in his voice: we ate three winters on bread we never bought.

The market inspector, the muhtasib, still made his rounds that winter with his scales and his ledger, because law does not stop being law when it becomes hard. The weight of a loaf was fixed. What some bakers did to that weight was their own affair between themselves and the ovens of a later Day: chalk in the flour, dust in the barley, loaves with clean faces and dirty hearts. Yunus weighed true. He could not have told you why it mattered so much to him, except that bread was the one sermon he knew how to give.

What he did instead was shrink the loaf. Not the weight the law fixed for a fals, that stayed honest to the grain. He shrank his own portioning, the margin every baker keeps for himself, the widow’s handful here, the cracked loaves there, the difference between what the oven made and what the house needed. He baked smaller for his own table so that the tray at the shop window could stay full longer into the afternoon, so that the last man in the line, the one with the look, would not have to turn around and tell his family a lie.

And then, because smallness has its own arithmetic, he began the night batch. After the last prayer, when the lane slept, he swept the day’s corners: bran, broken grain, the coarse siftings the pigeon keepers used to buy, the ends of barley the merchant let go for almost nothing because almost nothing was all Yunus offered. He kneaded it with the sour mother and a pinch of salt and baked it in the falling heat of the banked oven, rough loaves, dark and heavy and honest, bread with its sleeves rolled up.

Then he went out. There is an hour before the dawn prayer when Cairo belongs to the cats and the water carriers, and Yunus learned it by heart. He learned doors the way he knew dough, by feel: the schoolteacher who had not been paid since summer, the porter with six children and a back going crooked, the widow Umm Hasan whose cough came through her shutters like a slow drum. He set the loaves on the doorsteps and left. He was never once seen, or so he believed, and belief before dawn is easy.

Understand that he was not brave. His heart knocked at every corner. Some nights he stood in his own doorway with the basket on his arm and argued with himself in the dark: the jar is low, the winter is long, your children eat what you give away. He went anyway, not because the argument was won but because his feet had stopped listening to it. His father had loved one saying of the Prophet ﷺ above all others and had repeated it over the kneading trough for forty years: guard yourself from the Fire, even with half a date. Yunus had no dates. He had bran.

He paid for it where no one could see. He began eating his own supper short, then shorter. He mended his belt twice that winter, moving the buckle inward, and told Safiyya the leather had stretched. He drank warm water with a little salt at night, an old bakers’ trick against the hollow hour. Hunger, he discovered, is loud for three days and then becomes a companion, walking beside you with its hand on your shoulder, saying little.

The secrecy he kept for three reasons, though he could have named only one. For the takers, because shame is heavier than hunger, and a man who is seen receiving eats his bread with a bent neck. For himself, because he did not trust his own heart within a mile of praise. And for Safiyya, because she counted, and he could not face the count. This third reason he did not say even inwardly, but it set the hour of his errand as surely as the dawn set the hour of his prayer.

A loaf is a small thing. At the bottom of a hungry year it is not small. It is the difference between a child who sleeps and a child who cries himself there, and every mother on the lane could have told you which house had which.

Safiyya kept her ledger without paper. Inside the lid of the flour bin she made small charcoal strokes, one for every measure that left it, and at her waist she wore a cord in which she tied a knot for every coin that left the house. She knew dough the way Yunus knew fire, and by the middle of winter the numbers had stopped agreeing. The bin was falling faster than the family ate. Two measures a night, near enough, walking out of the house on their own legs.

She did not accuse him at once. She was a careful woman, and careful women check the sum twice. She lay still one night with her breathing slow and false, and heard him rise, and heard the basket, and heard the door. When he came back in the black cold before the dawn prayer, she was standing by the oven with the charcoal lid in her hand, and the look on her face was not anger. Anger would have been easier. It was fear, counted out in small strokes.

“I have weighed the children this winter,” she said, quietly, so as not to wake them. “Not on scales. On my arms. Dawud is lighter than he was at harvest. Ruqayya’s wrists, I can close my finger and thumb around them and there is room. You are a good man, Yunus, and you are pouring water out of a boat that is leaking. When the jar is empty, will the lane feed us? The lane cannot feed itself. I am not asking you to be cruel. I am asking you to be arithmetic.”

He had no answer that could stand up in the court she kept. He was not a scholar; he could not have argued provision from the Book with chapter and verse. All he had was a memory with flour on it. “When I was Dawud’s age,” he said, “someone fed us three winters and was never seen. My father died still praying for a man whose face he did not know. Somebody’s wife counted those measures, Safiyya. Somebody’s wife watched that flour walk out the door in the dark.” He looked at the lid in her hand. “I never wondered until tonight what she said to him.”

“Perhaps she said nothing,” said Safiyya, “and they starved in the spring, and were praised at their funeral.” The words came out harder than her face wanted them to. In the silence after, the widow’s cough came through the wall, slow and patient as a drum. Safiyya closed her eyes. “The children first,” she said. “Promise me the children eat first, whatever else you do.” It was not surrender, and it was not permission. It was a woman moving one plank of her boat to see if the sea truly came in.

He stopped for three nights, all the same, to honour her fear, and those were the longest nights of the winter. The house felt no fuller for it. He lay awake doing sums of his own, and found himself counting backwards for once: the fever Ruqayya had shaken off in autumn when the physician had waived his fee, shrugging, saying bakers’ children were his alms. The fuel merchant who had thrown a sack of dung cakes onto the cart unasked. The sour mother itself, forty years unbought. He had kept accounts of what left the house all his life without noticing that he had never once been the only one providing for it.

On the fourth morning he saw the gleaners at his ash pit, two children with a spoon, going through the cold cinders for crusts that had burnt and been thrown away. They were not from the lane. They did not beg. They worked the ash with the seriousness of clerks, and it was this, the seriousness, that finished him. He came home and said to Safiyya, to her face and in daylight, “I will bake the night batch from my own bowl. Not yours, not theirs. Mine. I can be hungry. I cannot be the man who watched.”

She looked at him for a long time, and then she did the thing he loved her for until the day he died: she reached into the bin, and added one small measure to his. “Someone in this house must count,” she said. “Then count everything,” he said. “Count what comes in, too.” She thought this was a foolish answer, that winter. She tied a second cord at her waist anyway, because she was accurate, and accuracy wants both columns.

movements.h: From Where He Did Not Expect
ps: Provision did not fall on the saddlers’ lane the way rain falls in stories, all at once and from straight above. It moved sideways, hand to hand, wearing faces and excuses, so that afterwards you could explain every part of it and still not be able to explain the whole. That is how it usually moves. The explanation is true, and it is not the truth.

It came first wearing the muhtasib’s dusty turban. In the worst month, the market inspector caught two bakers with chalk in their white flour and a third with weighted scales, and the lane watched them ride backwards through the market with their shame cried out before them. The same week, the amir’s storehouse opened a measure of grain for public bread, as rulers do when the mosques grow loud with the poor, and the inspector was told to choose ovens that could be trusted with other people’s flour. He did not deliberate long. “The one near the southern gate,” he said. “The one whose scales I have never had to touch. His bread is dark and his weights are clean.”

So the official grain came to Yunus’s oven, sacks of it on grey donkeys, and with it came a wage, paid in flour, which is the only coin a famine respects. The oven that had been banked to embers now burned from the dawn prayer to the night one, and the lane rediscovered a smell it had been mourning. Work, Yunus thought, standing in the roar of his own oven with his shirt soaked through in the middle of winter. No angel had handed him a purse. He had been handed labour, which is provision wearing an apron.

Heat itself became bread. The neighbours came shy at first, then not, to set their pots of beans in the falling warmth of the oven overnight, the old custom, and to sit against the warm wall with their children in the crook of their arms. The oven fed people it never fed, if you understand the arithmetic. A woman whose house has one warm wall in it does not spend her last strength shivering, and strength unspent is a meal nobody cooked.

Then it came wearing a letter. The widow Umm Hasan, it turned out, had not been asleep all those months ago. She had heard the basket and opened her shutter a finger’s width, and had seen exactly what the darkness was doing in her lane, and had kept the secret the way the poor keep the secrets of the generous, as treasure. She wrote to her son Salim, a clerk of weights in Alexandria, a young man of small salary and exact conscience. In spring a boat brought a sack of Rumi wheat with a letter tied to its neck: for the oven that does not sleep, from a son whose mother did not die this winter.

It arrived, and Safiyya would tell this part for the rest of her life, in the very week the amir’s grain was ending, when her first cord had grown heavy with knots and her nerve had begun to fray again. She stood in the doorway with the sack at her feet and the letter in her hand, and could not speak. Umm Hasan, watching from her own door, laughed until she coughed, and then told her everything: the shutter, the finger’s width, the basket, the man who thought the dark kept his secrets. “You married a thief,” said the widow. “I saw him with these eyes, stealing bread into houses.”

And behind all of it, farther away than any of them could see, it came wearing weather. That summer, in the far south past the cataracts, in highlands none of them would ever visit, rain fell. It fell for weeks on mountains they did not know the names of, and the water did what water has been commanded to do since the beginning: it gathered, it obeyed its slopes, it came down a thousand miles to find the fields of Egypt. The criers went up from the Nilometer, and this time their voices climbed, cubit by cubit, and the city wept at a number.

That night Safiyya sat late over her two cords, the leaving cord and the arriving cord, trying to make the winter balance the way an honest ledger should. The knots would not cooperate. Flour had left by measures; what had come back had come as a wage, a wall, a wheat sack, a waived fee, a rain a thousand miles away, none of it in units her fingers could tie. She laughed once, short, at her own hands, and said, “It will not balance. I cannot make it balance.” “It never balances,” said Yunus from the dark. “It overflows on one side. I stopped trying to catch it in a cup years ago. I just bake.”

The next year, when the flood came full and the drums beat at the cutting of the canal, and boys leapt into the brown water with their clothes on, Yunus stood at the back of the crowd like a man at a reunion. The loaves at his window had grown back to their old roundness, the way faces on the lane had. Dawud was suddenly tall, all elbows, and worked the peel beside his father. Ruqayya had appointed herself keeper of the sour mother and fed it every night with the seriousness of a clerk, folding today into tomorrow the way it had been done for sixty years.

On the first Friday after the flood, the khatib, the preacher, rose in the mosque near the southern gate and recited into the hush the verses of the chapter of divorce, of all places, the verses every poor man in Egypt carried like a coin sewn into a coat: whoever is mindful of Allah, He makes for him a way out, and provides for him from where he does not expect. And whoever leans his whole weight on Allah, He is enough for him. Yunus had heard the verses all his life. This time they read like his own household accounts, entered in a hand finer than Safiyya’s.

From where he does not expect. He sat with his rough hands open on his knees and walked back through the winter, door by door. Not one sack of it had come from where he had planned. He had planned only the giving away, the emptying side of the ledger. The filling had come sideways, through an inspector’s scales, a widow’s shutter, a clerk’s conscience, a wall’s warmth, and a rain in the far south that had been decreed before any of them was born. He had spent his whole life calling Allah the Provider with his tongue, one Name in a memorized string. It is a different thing to find the Name’s fingerprints on your own flour bin.

He never grew rich, in case you are waiting for that. The oven near the southern gate stayed small, and Yunus died an old man with flour in the creases of his hands and no property to divide except a jar of living dough, which Ruqayya took, and a copper basket, which Dawud took, and a custom, which the lane took and kept for a hundred years without remembering whose it was: in hard months, bread appeared on doorsteps before the dawn prayer, and no one saw it come, and everyone knew better than to look.

Safiyya outlived him, still accurate. She hung the two cords on a nail by the door where the winter light caught them, the heavy one and the light one, and when her grandchildren asked she would run her thumb along the knots like a woman reading. “This one is everything the house gave away in the famine year,” she would say. “And this one is everything that came. I tied them both myself, so I can tell you honestly which string ran out first.” Then she would hang them back on the nail, leaving the question standing in the room, doing its quiet work.
The oven cooled every night of its life. The Providing never did.

ayah.ar: وَمَن يَتَّقِ اللَّهَ يَجْعَل لَّهُ مَخْرَجًا ﴿٢﴾ وَيَرْزُقْهُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَحْتَسِبُ ۚ وَمَن يَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ فَهُوَ حَسْبُهُ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ بَالِغُ أَمْرِهِ ۚ قَدْ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدْرًا ﴿٣﴾
ayah.en: And whoever is mindful of Allah, He makes for him a way out, and provides for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, He is enough for him. Indeed, Allah accomplishes His purpose. Allah has set a measure for every thing.

stories.epigraph: He weighed the flour every night of his life; he never once managed to weigh the Giver.

stories.title: The Calligrapher’s Last Qur’an
stories.setting: Samarkand, early 1400s, in the city of blue domes and paper mills
stories.reader_note: For anyone whose life’s work came out smaller than the dream, and who has quietly filed that smallness under failure.

ps: Samarkand in those years was a city being written. Masons went up the ribbed domes like ants on blue fruit, setting tiles the colour of deep water, and along the canal the paper mills thumped day and night, beating mulberry bark into the finest paper in the world, sheets you could hold to the sun and read the light through. Ink came into the gates in jars, lapis came in from the mountains for the blue of headings, gold came in for the gold. A city can be famous for bread or for horses. This one was famous for the written word, and knew it.

In a narrow shop off the booksellers’ row worked Tahir ibn Mahmud, a copyist of the Qur’an for fifty of his sixty-six years. He had cut his first reed pen at nine, under his father’s eye, and had been measuring his letters ever since by the old discipline: the diamond dot the pen makes when touched once to paper, so many dots to an alif, so many to the bowl of a nun, beauty ruled like law and free inside it. His naskh, the round clear script of Qur’ans, was known as far as Herat. Students copied his pages the way archers study a master’s release.

His tools were few and old. Reed pens seasoned in his cupboard for years before he would cut them, a knife with a worn ivory handle, a burnisher of agate, soot ink he ground himself with gum and gall, mixed slow, in the old proportion. Paper he chose the way other men choose land. He worked cross-legged at a low desk with the page on his raised knee, and between the dipping of the pen and the touch of the nib there was a stillness in him that apprentices noticed and could not copy, because it cannot be taught by watching.

He had buried a wife and a daughter, years ago, in one bad summer, and had not remarried. What remained to him was the craft, an apprentice called Iskandar who had good hands and a better heart, and one desire, kept where other men keep money. He wished, before he died, to write a great mushaf, a full copy of the Qur’an, for the royal library. Vellum-sized pages, gold rosettes between the verses, a binding worth a village. Not for the fee. He wanted his best hour to stand in the best company, shelved among the masters, and be read there when he was dust.

It was not a wicked wish. Say it plainly: it was the wish of every honest craftsman, that the work should land where the work deserves. He had served it patiently. He had outlived two court calligraphers and trained the pupils of a third, and word had begun to move in the booksellers’ row, the way water moves under ice, that when the new madrasa was finished and its library endowed, the commission of commissions would at last come down the hill, and that the old man in the narrow shop had earned it twice over.

His mother, dead now fifty years, had taught him his first habit of the trade, before any master taught him the second. When the reed split clean and the ink sat well, she would tap his small wrist and whisper: say alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. Thanks is water on a seed, my son. What you thank Him for, He grows. He had said it then because she said it. Somewhere along the road of becoming excellent, the habit had worn thin, the way a coin loses its face from long handling. The words still fell from him at the right moments. They had stopped landing anywhere.

It began, as endings do, with almost nothing. A Thursday in early winter, cold light on the page, and the downstroke of an alif, the letter he had drawn perhaps a million times, came out with a waver in it, fine as a hair, visible to no eye in the city except his. He put down the pen and looked at his right hand as if it belonged to a stranger who had wandered into the shop. It lay quiet. He drank warm water, blamed the cold, rewrote the page, and said nothing to Iskandar.

But the waver came back, and brought relatives. Some days his hand was his own until noon and then hummed like a plucked string. Some days it woke trembling and settled by midmorning, so that he learned to bargain with it, hour by hour, the way you bargain with a moneylender. He hid it well. He was a master; he had forty tricks for steadiness, the braced little finger, the slowed breath, the letter built from shorter pulls. The tricks bought him a year. They could not buy back the thing that had left, which was certainty, the body’s silent yes on which a lifetime of beauty had stood.

The commission of commissions came down the hill that spring, as the row had said it would. It went to Ghiyas, a man of thirty-four with a hand like running silk, who had been, twenty years before, a boy grinding soot in Tahir’s shop. They said his muhaqqaq script, the tall stately script of royal Qur’ans, was the finest in a generation. They were right, which made it worse. Ghiyas came himself, out of respect, awkward at the door with the guilt of the beloved, and Tahir served him tea with a steady enough hand and praised him, and meant it, and felt, under the meaning, a floor give way.
The pen had been his tongue. Now he stammered.

That summer he began to set his affairs in the direction of silence. He sold two bolts of stored paper. He arranged for Iskandar to finish the outstanding wedding contracts and Fatiha panels, small jobs, jobs a shaking man could hand off without shame. He oiled the ivory knife and put it away in its cloth, and understood, watching his own hands fold the cloth, that he was performing a funeral, one item at a time, for a man still breathing.

In those weeks his gratitude, the worn coin, went from thin to counterfeit. He prayed as always, prostrating on the old reed mat until his forehead knew its weave, but inside the prayers he was drafting complaints. Fifty years, he told the darkness. Fifty years of Your Book, letter by letter, and at the door of the library You took my hand from me. He was too old and too honest to dress the feeling in prettier clothes. It was grievance, and he knew its name, and could not put it down.

He did not stop believing. Belief was the bone of him; you might as well ask a mountain to stop. But there is a kind of sorrow that sits down between a man and his Lord like fog between two houses. The houses do not move. The fog does not lift by wishing. And every morning the paper mills thumped along the canal, making beautiful blank pages for other men’s hands, and the blue domes went on rising over a city that wrote and wrote and no longer needed him to.

The imam came in the month of Rajab, in from the Zarafshan hills with the wool smell of the high pastures still on his coat, an oldish man with rain-cracked hands who stood in the doorway of the shop turning his cap like a boy. His village was three days up the valley, past the last mill. It had a mosque of poplar beams, a stream, four hundred sheep, and now, at last, by the mercy of Allah and eleven years of set-aside coins, a school. Forty children. He had come down the mountain to buy what a school of the Qur’an cannot be without.

He laid his money on the desk in a knotted cloth, and it was, to be plain, the price of good paper and not much beyond. He knew it. The cap went round and round in his hands. He had been to two shops already and been quoted politely out the door. Someone in the row, perhaps in mischief, perhaps in something better dressed than mischief, had said: go to the old man near the end, his prices have become strange lately. And so he stood, asking the finest naskh hand between here and Herat for a small plain mushaf, a schoolroom copy, to be handled by forty pairs of unwashed hands until it fell apart.

Tahir heard him out and felt the insult arrive on schedule, right on the sore. A schoolbook. A goat-track Qur’an. The library on the hill was being fitted, that very season, with lamps of pierced brass for Ghiyas’s pages, and here at his desk stood sheep-smell and a knotted cloth, offering him the one commission left on earth. He opened his mouth to say what the other shops had said, gently, that his eyes were failing, that his time was sold ahead.

The imam, sensing the shape of the coming no, spoke first, not cleverly, just from his life. “They tell me the great library will have a hundred Qur’ans,” he said. “Locked, praise Allah, behind lattice doors, kept beautiful. My school has forty children and not one. Whatever you write, master, will be read to pieces. I cannot promise it a shelf. I can promise it will never once be lonely.” Then, ashamed of his own eloquence, he looked down at his cracked hands and added, “And we would pray for the writer. Up there, prayer is mostly what we have.”

Afterwards Tahir could not fully explain, even to himself, why he did not refuse; only that the words read to pieces had gone in like a splinter and would not come out. He heard himself name a fee that matched the knotted cloth, saw the imam’s face open like weather clearing, and was committed before his grievance could organize a defense. When the man had gone, Iskandar looked a question at him. “Charity,” said Tahir, gruffly, and believed it. He was wrong about that. It was not what he was giving. It was what he was about to be given.

That night he took stock of his enemy honestly, as a craftsman should. The tremor was worst when he was tired, worst of all when he was bitter, and mildest, he had noticed without ever using the knowledge, in the first hour after the dawn prayer, when the shop was cold and the street silent and the ink smelled of its beginnings. One steady hour, most days. Out of the wreck of a great career, one good hour had been left to him, the way a fire leaves one beam standing.

A younger man would have measured that hour against the library and despaired. Tahir measured it against forty children who had never held a Qur’an, and found, doing that sum, that the fog between the two houses had thinned very slightly, for the first time since Thursday in early winter. He did not yet call this by any Name. He only cut, that evening, with great slowness, a new pen.

He built his last work the way the poor build houses, out of exactly what was there. Each day began in the dark: the ablution, the dawn prayer with Iskandar at the neighbourhood mosque, then the shop, the lamp, the page tilted on his knee. Before the first dip of the pen he made himself say his mother’s words, alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah, and say them slowly, landing them one by one, like a man laying coins on a table rather than throwing them. Praise for the hour. For the paper. For the black of the ink. For a hand quiet enough, this morning, to serve.

It had begun as a discipline against bitterness, a fence for his own heart. Within a month it had become the architecture of the whole book. He found that thanks, said slowly, did to his hour what the agate burnisher did to paper: pressed it smooth, closed its pores, made it take ink cleanly. On the days he began with the ledger of his losses, the tremor arrived early, feeding on the agitation like fire on draught. On the days he began with the small accounting of what remained, the hand stayed his own, sometimes clear to midmorning. His body, it turned out, had been listening to his heart all along.

So he thanked his way through the Book. He wrote the Opening, the Fatiha, in an hour so still he heard the ink dry. He learned to stop at the first hum of the tremor, mid-word if need be, without anger, setting the pen down as you set down a sleeping child, and to fill the shaking hours with the parts of the craft that shaking permits: grinding soot, ruling lines with the cord, teaching Iskandar the cutting of reeds, sitting in the doorway with tea, watching the street the way old men watch fires. The illness had shrunk his art to one hour. Gratitude was quietly teaching him how much of a life fits inside one hour.

Twice that year the hand failed badly and pages were lost, and the old grief came up the stairs of him like flood water. Both times he went out and walked the booksellers’ row to the open square and stood in the crowd’s noise until the worst passed, and both times, coming back, he did the same strange arithmetic on the doorstep: still the dawn hour, still the paper, still the boy, still the Book. Not once did the column come up empty. He began to suspect, shyly, like a man suspecting he is loved, that it never had.

He made the schoolbook plainly, as commissioned, but plainness in a master’s hand is its own wealth. Small pages, a clear open naskh a child’s finger could follow line by line without drowning, margins wide enough for forty years of teachers’ pencil marks, paper chosen to endure handling, thread sewn double. No gold. In place of gold he spent what he actually had: fifty years of knowing exactly how a letter should sit so that the eye rests on it. The great library would have its hundred glories behind lattice. This one was built the way you build a boat, for water, not for the harbour.

He finished on a night in early autumn, alone, past midnight, Iskandar asleep in the back of the shop. The last lines of the last surah, the one that begins say: He is Allah, the One, then the two surahs of refuge, and then it was done, and he sat looking at the wet ink with his heart doing something for which the only old word is gratitude, the full kind, the kind with awe in it. On the final leaf, where a master sets his name and titles, he wrote no name. He wrote only: the work of a hand that shook, for hands that are small. Alhamdulillah, wa alhamdulillah, wa alhamdulillah.

He woke Iskandar for the dawn prayer, and they went out together into the blue cold and prayed, and came back, and Tahir sat down at his desk before the finished book, saying he would rest a moment before wrapping it. The light came up over the booksellers’ row the way it does in that city, hitting the high domes first, turquoise catching fire, and then sliding down the walls into the ordinary streets. It crossed the desk. It crossed the drying page. Iskandar, grinding the morning ink, heard his master say, distinctly, contentedly, the word he now began everything with. When he turned, the old man’s eyes were closed, and the hour, the steady hour, had been left open like a door, and Tahir ibn Mahmud had gone through it.
There are worse deaths than at your desk, at dawn, past a finished Qur’an, with praise as your last word and no debts behind you. There may not be many better.

He was washed, shrouded and prayed over that afternoon, with the booksellers’ row standing close and Ghiyas of the silken hand weeping openly at the front, and he was in the ground before sunset, as is the sunnah, the Prophet’s ﷺ way, buried in the cemetery outside the walls where the paper-mill workers are buried, which he would have liked. Iskandar closed the shop for three days. On the fourth he wrapped the small mushaf in waxed cloth and oiled leather, and walked it up the valley himself, three days past the last mill, and put it into the imam’s rain-cracked hands, and would take nothing for it except breakfast.

Now watch what Tahir never saw. The book was set on a low wooden stand in a room of poplar beams, and that winter forty children learned the shapes of the letters from its wide clear lines, their fingers moving under the words like small boats. Among them was a shepherd’s son called Sanjar, slow at everything except this, who at eleven had the Fatiha, at fourteen the last thirtieth of the Book, and at twenty had all of it, the whole Qur’an standing upright in his chest, learned entire from one plain copy with no gold in it. He became the school’s teacher when the old imam died. He taught for forty-one years.

The book was rebound the first time in Sanjar’s middle age, in goatskin, by a binder down the valley who, seeing the colophon, the closing inscription, would not take payment either: the work of a hand that shook, for hands that are small. It was rebound again in his successor’s time, and again two generations later, its first pages worn soft as cloth, the corner of the Fatiha darkened by two hundred years of small right thumbs, and mended, and darkened again. Teachers came to know its pages so well they could tell you where every water stain sat, the way you know the scars on your own family.

War came up the valley once a century, as it does, and took sheep, roofs, and twice the mosque itself. The book spent one bad year buried in a shepherd’s lambing cave, wrapped in the waxed cloth, and came out smelling of wool, unharmed. The great library on the hill was scattered in the troubles of a later age, its hundred glories sold, burned, or carried away to cities that catalogued them beautifully. Lattice doors keep out hands, it turns out, but not history. Love is the better fortress. A thing that four hundred people would die before surrendering is safer than anything behind brass.

Count it now, the way Safiyya the baker’s wife would have counted it, if you have read that story: one steady hour a day, for one year, from one shaking man, multiplied. Thousands of children, well past all numbering, learned to read the speech of their Lord from that one plain book, and taught it onward, so that on quiet mornings in that valley to this day there is a sound like bees that is actually the Qur’an, being recited by small voices, all of them downstream of an old man who thought his life had failed because it ended small. He asked to be shelved among the masters. He was granted, instead, an unpayable wage: he was made useful after death, and is being paid to this hour.

The village prays for the writer still, by his colophon, since it left them no name. And here at last is the Name that was working all along, the one his mother had watered him with, seed by seed: Ash-Shakur, the Most Appreciative, the One who does not merely accept small deeds but thanks His servants for them, and pays them out at a rate no market on earth could survive, a rate that turns one steady hour into two hundred years. People imagine He is hard to please. The whole story of the small Qur’an of the Zarafshan valley says otherwise. He is astonishingly easy to please. He is only impossible to outgive.

ayah.ar: لِيُوَفِّيَهُمْ أُجُورَهُمْ وَيَزِيدَهُم مِّن فَضْلِهِ ۚ إِنَّهُ غَفُورٌ شَكُورٌ
ayah.en: That He may pay them their wages in full and increase them from His bounty. Indeed, He is Forgiving, Most Appreciative.

stories.epigraph: He thanked Allah for one steady hour, and the hour has outlived him by two hundred years.

stories.title: The Du’a That Outlived Her
stories.setting: Timbuktu and the Sahara, 1500s, on the salt roads of the desert
stories.reader_note: For the one who walked away, and for the one who never stopped asking Allah about them by name.

movements.h: The House of Books and Salt
ps: Timbuktu in those years stood where the desert and the river agree to meet and trade. Out of the north came salt, cut at the flats of Taghaza in slabs like grey marble, two to a camel. Up from the river port came gold dust folded in feather quills, cloth, kola nuts, dried fish and grain. And through the middle of it, holding its own against salt and gold, moved the city’s third currency, which was books. Scholars taught in the shade of the great mud-brick mosques. Scribes copied by lamplight. A good manuscript could buy a camel. A great one could buy the herd.

Idris was born into a house that handled two of the three. His father traded salt, and his mother, Maryam, had married into the trade from a family of scribes, and could recite more of the Qur’an than many men who taught it. Their house near the Sankore mosque had a flat roof for sleeping in the hot months, a courtyard acacia, and a wooden chest of books which his mother dusted with the reverence other women in the quarter kept for gold. The call to prayer came over the rooftops five times a day like a tide, and the house rose to it, easily, as boats rise.

The boy learned as boys there learned: letters chalked on a whitewashed wooden board, verses recited until they sat firm, then the board washed and the next verses written over the ghosts of the last. He had a quick mind and quicker feet. His father would set him small sums of the trade, so many slabs at Taghaza, so many mithqals of gold at the river, and the boy would have the answer before the question ended. His mother, watching, held her praise the way careful people hold coins. She had seen quickness before. Quickness, she said once, gets a man to the wrong place early.

His father died when Idris was seventeen, on the road home from the mines, of a fever that took three days and a lifetime. The caravan brought his salt back untouched, every slab accounted for, because desert men do not steal from the dead: the sum of a man came home walking beside his camels, goods intact, owner gone. Idris stood at the grave beside his mother and understood that he was now the house. What he did not notice, being seventeen and full of the future, was that somewhere in him a quiet clerk had written, and underlined, that roads pay and prayer does not.

Maryam saw it, the way mothers see hairline cracks in cups they know. She said little. She was not a woman of lectures but of habits: the night prayer when the house slept, the dawn prayer never missed, the Book out of the chest at first light. Her voice doing its slow recitation was the sound Idris woke to all his childhood, the way other children wake to roosters. Later, in the years when he had stopped answering her letters, it was this sound, more than her face, that would come back to him at bad moments, arriving unasked across a thousand miles of sand.

For a while the young man kept the shape of his father’s religion, prayer at the edges of business, alms when the season was fat. But shapes without weight drift. Fajr, the dawn prayer, went first, traded one morning for sleep after a late arrival, then the next morning, then simply gone, the way a tent peg works loose in soft ground: no single night you could name, and then the whole corner of the roof is down. By twenty-two, the only prostration left in his life was the camel’s, kneeling to take on salt.

He was, let it be said honestly, brilliant at the trade. He learned the roads the way he had learned sums: wells and waypoints and the politics of wells, when to buy salt cheap at the flats and when to hold it until the price stood up on its hind legs. He took his father’s middling business and in ten years made it a name. Twenty camels became sixty, then two hundred. He built a second house near the market with doors of studded wood, and men at the port began to say his name with the small pause that means money.

His mother stayed in the old house by Sankore and would not be moved into the new one. When he visited, which was often at first, she would feed him rice and river fish and ask nothing about prices. She asked other things. Whether he prayed. Whether he had eaten among the poor lately. Whether he was sleeping. He answered the last question and slid past the others with jokes, and she let him, and prayed the night prayers over his name instead. He knew she did. Everyone knew. It half touched and half chafed him, like a garment from home that no longer quite fit.

The chafing won. The year he turned thirty, drought sat on the land, and his mother fasted and prayed with the fervour of the whole quarter. Idris, meaning it kindly, said the thing he spent thirty years unable to unsay: ask your Lord for rain, mother, and leave my affairs to me. I have guides for the desert and clerks for the sums. Gold answers faster. She looked at him a long, level moment, and answered without heat, the way she said everything: gold is a good servant on the road, my son. But gold cannot find the road home. I will keep asking the One who made you.

He laughed, kissed her hands, and went back to his camels, and their two sentences stood facing each other across the next twenty years like markers on opposite banks. She did keep asking. Every Friday, the neighbours knew, and in the last third of every night: not for his wealth, never once for his wealth, but with one strange stubborn request she wore like a ring: O Allah, Guide of the lost, bring him home by any road You choose. The wording frightened her sister, who said, you do not know what you are permitting. Maryam kept the wording. Mothers who pray at night know exactly what they are permitting.

When he left that season for the mines, she gave him what she always gave, provisions and blessing, and one thing more: paper folded to the size of a thumb, sewn shut in a scrap of red leather. He turned it over, amused. A charm, mother? From you? Her mouth went firm. It is not a charm, she said. Charms are for people who think secrets do the work. It is a letter: it asks nothing of the leather and everything of Allah. Open it when you are lost. He said, smiling, I have the best guides in the desert. She said, I know. Open it when you are lost.

He carried it because refusing was more trouble than carrying. It went into the corner of his saddle bag with flint and needles, the small republic of forgotten things, and stayed there through every crossing for twenty years, sewn shut, unread, riding a hand’s width from his hip the whole length of every road he took away from her. Later he would understand that this was the truest picture of those years anyone could have drawn: her word that close, and him never once reaching for it.

movements.h: News Travels at the Speed of Camels
ps: The years themselves can be told quickly, because he spent them quickly. Salt north to south, gold south to north, cloth and books both ways. Two marriages, both correct, neither warm; no children living past their second year, a grief he filed under the will of God with a clerk’s efficiency and never opened again. Feasts for men he did not like. The hajj postponed decade by decade, always the year after next. His mother’s letters came by caravan, dictated to a scribe, short and unchanging: I am well. The quarter is well. I ask Allah to guide you and to let me see your face. He sent back silver and no sentences.

He was north at the flats, watching salt come white out of the ground, the year the letter arrived that was not from her. Her neighbour’s son had written it, in a careful student hand: that Maryam bint Ahmad had died in Ramadan, on a Friday, at dawn, with her Book beside her; that half the quarter had prayed over her; that she was buried by the wall of the old cemetery; and that among her last words had been his name, and these: tell him it is not too late. The letter had taken four months to find him. She was four months buried before he knew the world had changed.

He read it standing in the white glare of the flats, and what he felt was the most frightening thing he had ever felt, which was nothing. A whiteness, like the flats. He paid for mourning cloth. He sent money for the grave to be tended and a wall repaired in her name. He fed the miners lavishly that night in her honour, and the men praised his devotion, and he lay awake hearing them praise it. He could not weep. He told himself grief was for men with time, and took the next caravan, and was very brilliant for three more years, the way a spun coin is upright just before the end.

It is not too late. He decided the words were a dying woman’s tenderness and forbade them the premises. They came in anyway, at their own hours, usually at dawn, which stubbornly went on arriving every day, her hour, the hour of the voice doing its slow recitation over the rooftops of his childhood. He began to be known, those years, as a hard man to wake before mid-morning.

In his fifty-first year he assembled the largest caravan of his life, four hundred camels for the autumn salt, and rode north with it himself, which the clerks thought needless and the young men thought magnificent. He could not have told you why he went in person. The trade did not need him. Perhaps, though he would have cursed the suggestion, some part of him had begun listening for something out there in the silence between wells, and wanted to be present when it spoke.

The guide on that road was a Tuareg of perhaps sixty called Amastan, veiled to the eyes in the indigo cloth of his people, so spare of speech that the drivers said he paid for each word out of his own water ration. He read sand the way scholars read margins: the grain of the dunes under the wind, the colour of distance, the taste of earth from a dry well. Idris hired him as he hired everyone, as an instrument, and noticed him twice in the first ten days: once when he corrected their line by three fingers against the sunset, and once at prayer.

It was the prayer that first snagged on Idris, small as a thorn. Whatever the day was doing, Amastan prayed it on time. He would swing down, sweep a place clear with his forearm, purify himself with sand in the manner the Law allows where water is life itself, the dry ablution, and stand facing across the dunes, unhurried, as if the open desert were the courtyard of his house. The caravan flowed around him; he never once looked up to see whether it waited. Idris, watching from the saddle with thirty years of unprayed prayers stacked behind his ribs, found the sight obscurely infuriating, and could not stop watching.

Nine days short of the mines, the wind changed. Amastan smelled it before the sky admitted anything; he turned his face north like a man reading bad news over another man’s shoulder, and gave quiet orders: water tight, camels coupled, cloth ready. The storm came up from the horizon in the late afternoon, a brown wall with its own weather inside it, and then there was no sky, no line, no north, only sand moving like a live thing and the world shrunk to the reach of your arm. They knelt the camels and lay against them and let it scream. It screamed for two days.

When it ended, the desert had been rewritten. Dunes were gone, dunes were new, the track was a rumour, and the stars came out that night over a country no map had met. They walked the camels slow while Amastan cast for signs, and on the second day Idris heard the words a desert man will spend anything not to say, said quietly, with the accounts exact: the storm has carried us east of the line. The forward well is lost somewhere behind the wind. Water in the skins, five days, six with mercy. The men took the news silently, each privately beginning to pray.

That evening, with the sun going down bloody over sand that belonged to no one, Amastan swung down from his camel, swept the ground clear with his forearm, and stood to pray the sunset prayer, on time, exactly as always. And something in Idris tore loose from thirty years of moorings. He heard his own voice, cracked with dust and fear and something older than both, shouting across the cooling air: at this you pray? You do not even know where the qibla is. You do not know where anything is. We are lost, old man, or has that news not reached you?

Amastan finished the prayer completely, unhurried, turning his face right and left with the salutation of peace. Then he rose, and looked at the merchant, and paid out four of his words. I am lost, he said. He is not.

He mounted and rode on, leaving the sentence standing in the open desert, and Idris sat his saddle in the red light unable to move, a rich man with four hundred camels of salt and five days of water, hearing his whole life described in one breath by a stranger. Lost, and guided, were real words, then. Conditions, not figures of speech. A man could be one and not the other. A man could be lost long before any storm, and the storm only said it aloud.

That night he could not sleep, and did not try. He sat apart from the fires with his saddle bag in his lap like a man holding an animal he fears, and some hours past midnight, in the enormous silence the desert keeps between winds, his hand went in among the flint and the needles and found the scrap of red leather, sewn shut, twenty years old, soft with riding. He cut the stitches with his thumbnail. Inside, in a fine scribe’s hand she had paid for with her cooking pots for all he knew, on paper that had crossed the Sahara at his hip forty times unread, was her letter.

It was short. It was not addressed to him. In the Name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. O Allah, Guide of the lost, You see my son, and I no longer do. He has forgotten the road, but You have never once lost sight of him. I am not asking You to make him rich; he will manage that, and it will not help him. I ask You for his heart. Bring him home by any road You choose, though it be long, though I be dead on the day he arrives. O Allah, let my boy die knowing You. And below, in the same borrowed hand, small as a seed: your mother, who is not lost, waiting.

The desert at night is the quietest room on earth, and in it a big man in his fifties made the sounds a boy makes, and no one came, because desert men know that some storms a man must stand in alone. Thirty years came down more or less at once. Dawn found him on his knees on the swept sand, doing what he had watched Amastan do, clumsily, out of practice in his very bones, forehead down on the cool ground, finding, when he reached for the Opening chapter, the Fatiha, that every word was still there. The words had waited in his mouth like a key, kept for him by Someone certain he would one day stand before the right door.

Guide us along the straight path. He had recited that line ten thousand boyhood mornings without hearing it. Now, lost in the exact and unfigurative sense, he heard it, and understood that he had been saying it all his life the way the drowned say water.

What happened next was not magic, and the story insists on this the way his mother would have. The wind had fallen in the night. The morning stood clean to the very edge of the world, one of a dozen such mornings a season, and in that hard clarity Amastan, casting west from a high dune since first light, went still, then came down at a run. Far off, a scarp of black rock whose shape he knew, a marker his grandfather’s grandfather had named. He had the line. Two days, he said. The water would be bitter and shallow and enough. The camels moaned as they rose, the caravan turned, and the man who had wept all night rode on, for the first time in thirty years, on a bearing someone trustworthy had set.

They watered at the bitter well, made the mines, loaded the salt, and came home by the long safe road, and the trade was profitable, and Idris found he did not care, in a new and unfrightening way. Outside the city he did what returning traders do not do: he dismounted, gave his riding camel to the youngest driver, and walked the last miles into Timbuktu on foot, through the gardens, past the port road, into the smell of dust and smoke and river that meant mother, and the men with him kept their questions, because his face was the face of a man arriving at something.

The old cemetery lies along a wall the colour of the desert it argues with. Her grave was kept, as his silver had arranged, plastered smooth, modest, right in every particular, and that correctness nearly undid him: everything paid for, nothing attended. He sat beside it in the afternoon dust like a boy outside a door and told her, in an undertone, with long pauses, about the storm, the guide, the letter, the key kept in his mouth. What the dead are given of our news, the scholars say cautiously, is Allah’s affair. He talked anyway. Some accounts want reading aloud.

It was her neighbour, ancient now, blind in one eye, who completed the ledger that evening, in the shade of the old courtyard where the acacia still stood. Every Friday, son. Every Friday of thirty years, and in the night we heard her through the wall. Never money, never even your health, strange woman, rahimaha Allah, may Allah have mercy on her. Only: Ya Hadi, O Guide, bring him home by any road You choose. She turned her seeing eye on him. You took the long one, she said, without malice, the way the old state weather. He said, yes. He had stopped defending himself against true sentences.

In the weeks after, he went to a teacher at the Sankore mosque and laid the matter before him like goods on a mat: the mother, the du’a, the thirty years, the storm, and the guilt that had ridden home with him, that she had died unanswered, his lateness having defeated her asking. The teacher listened to the end. Then he opened the Book to the chapter of the Stories, Surat al-Qasas, and read: you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills.

That was said, he added quietly, to the Prophet ﷺ himself, grieving a man he loved whose heart he could not turn. Understand, then, what your mother always understood. Guidance was never in her gift, nor in any created hand. She could not bring you home, and she knew it; that is exactly why she spent thirty years asking the One who can. Your return is not her defeat, merchant. It is her answer, arriving.

He lived another two decades, and the quarter came to know him the way it had known her. The big house near the market filled with other people’s children learning letters on whitewashed boards; he paid teachers the way he had once paid guides, and sat in at the back like a large late student, moving his lips. He prayed the dawn prayer in her mosque, at her hour, and was easy to wake. He went at last on the postponed hajj and wept at strange moments, at wells mostly, which the young pilgrims did not understand. And every Friday an old trader sat by a plastered grave near the wall, opening the week’s accounts aloud to the Auditor of all his roads.

They buried him there in the end, beside her, a small stone at the head. The stone gives no titles and records no camels. It says what he asked it to say, the sum of the whole ledger, four words for the caravans of the future to price if they can: lost, and then found.

ayah.ar: إِنَّكَ لَا تَهْدِي مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يَشَاءُ ۚ وَهُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِالْمُهْتَدِينَ
ayah.en: Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills, and He knows best those who will accept guidance.

stories.epigraph: I am lost, said the guide, finishing his prayer. He is not.

stories.title: The Setting of Broken Things
stories.setting: Sarajevo, the 1990s siege and the long years after
stories.reader_note: For anyone whose hands went on working long after something inside them went quiet.

ps: Tarik was twenty-nine the winter the city closed, a junior orthopedic surgeon with good hands and a plan for his life that assumed, as plans do, the continued existence of ordinary things: electricity, examinations, summer. By December the ordinary things had left the city one by one, and what remained was work. The hospital ran its operating theatres on generator hours and daylight, moved beds away from the windowed walls, and learned to do modern medicine by lamplight and improvisation, the way you learn anything, which is because you must, that day, with that patient, now.

His trade was bones, and the winter was generous to his trade in the worst way. People fell running across open crossings. People were dug from stairwells that had folded on them. Old women broke hips on ice no one salted anymore, salt, like everything, having become precious. He set what could be set: traction rigged from window weights, plaster hoarded like flour and stretched with care, frames of steel rods standing scaffold over shins the winter had ruined. When the X-ray film ran out, as it did for weeks at a time, he read fractures with his fingertips, the old way, closing his eyes to see.

There is a mercy built into surgical work which surgeons do not advertise: while your hands are inside the hour, the hour is all there is. The mind narrows to the field, the bone, the angle, the next right move. Fear waits politely outside the theatre door, and so does grief, and so, Tarik would learn, does everything else you are not doing about your own life. He operated, those months, more than some surgeons do in a decade. People called it dedication and were not wrong. It was also, quietly, the only room in the city where he could not hear the hills.

Home was a flat shared with his mother, Emina, and his brother, Kenan, nineteen that winter, who had been about to begin engineering studies when history cancelled the semester. Their father was six years dead of his heart, which the brothers had privately come to speak of, that winter, as a kind of luck. The flat’s windows were skinned with the humanitarian plastic sheeting that had replaced glass all over the city; the stove burned parquet slats and the corpses of books nobody could bring themselves to name aloud. Water came by hand, in canisters, from wherever water was that week.

Kenan carried the water. It was his job in the household economy and he had elevated it into a calling. He knew which lines were shortest, which crossings the cold light favoured, the exact number of steps home with two full canisters, twenty litres a side, and he announced records the way sportsmen do. He was the kind of nineteen the siege had made in quantity: an adult by necessity with a boy still living inside him like a subtenant. In the evenings the brothers played chess by candle, an old running battle neither dominated for long, and their mother watched them over her prayer beads, thanking her Lord in a whisper for two heads bent over a board.

Emina prayed through that winter the way other people kept diaries, five times a day and in the night, unhurried, in the cellar when the shelling was bad, in the kitchen when it was not. Tarik had drifted from all that at university, without drama, the way a man’s collar loosens through a long day. He did not mock it. Once, coming home grey at dawn after a night of casualties, he stood in the doorway and watched his mother’s forehead touch the floor of a city under siege, and felt something he had no shelf for: not faith exactly, but envy of the posture. He was too tired to think about it, and then it was spring.

If you had asked him what held him together that winter, he would have said, in the city’s dry way: routine, coffee substitute, and my brother’s chess problems. Roasted barley in the coffee pot. The generator’s two hours. Kenan’s opening trap, refuted for the hundredth time. A man does not always know what his load-bearing walls are. He finds out the way buildings find out.

It was a Tuesday in the second spring. There had been a lull for some days, one of those silences the city had learned not to trust and could not help trusting, because hope is a habit older than shelling. Kenan went for water in the morning with both canisters and his good mood, and at the door he promised his mother fresh bread if the bakery had managed anything, and told his brother, over his shoulder, laughing, that tonight he had a new opening prepared, something unanswerable, from a book. The door closed on the laugh. It is the last fact of him the flat ever held.

The morning went. The early afternoon went. What came instead of Kenan, toward evening, was a neighbour from the lower street, carrying one canister, full, which he set down inside the doorway with a terrible courtesy, and could not manage much beyond the essential words. There had been the lull, and then, at the water line, in one instant, the lull’s end. Several families on the lower street had such words delivered that evening. The second canister was never found. Tarik was at the hospital unloading casualties when the shells came in four streets away, and did not learn for two hours that one of the names moving through the corridors was his own.

He did not see his brother; a colleague, out of a mercy Tarik spent years deciding whether to be grateful for, arranged that he did not have to. The funeral was the next dusk, quick and quiet as siege funerals had to be, in the corner of a park that had become, like other green places in that city, a field of raw new markers, the old cemeteries being unreachable. Dusk, so the light would offer the hills nothing to work with. A handful of neighbours, a hurried imam, his mother upright in a way that cost more than wailing. Tarik stood with a clod of earth in his hand and felt the whiteness come down over him like theatre lights failing.

Here is what the whiteness was like. He set a stranger’s forearm at eight the next morning, correctly. His brother had gone into the ground at six the previous evening. Both facts were true, and they would not speak to each other, then or for years. Between them a wall went up in him overnight, mortarless, perfect, and behind it lived everything he could not afford: the opening from the book, never shown; the bread, never bought; the boy subtenant in the man; the twenty litres a side. In front of the wall lived a surgeon, functioning beautifully.

His mother grieved in the open, terribly and cleanly, the way her faith had taught her: tears without protest, protest without blasphemy, to Allah we belong and to Him we return, said not as a formula but as a road walked daily on the knees. She wept; she prayed; she said her son’s name aloud at will. Tarik could do none of those things and did not try. He worked. When the neighbours praised his strength, his mother looked at her surviving son with an expression he refused to read, because reading it would have meant knowing that she had two broken children now, and could reach only one of them.

The chessboard stayed as it was, mid-game, on the shelf above the stove, Kenan’s knight deep in enemy territory on a mission now permanently classified. Neither mother nor son ever spoke of it, and neither ever moved a piece, and the pieces stood there through the rest of the war, through the strange loud peace, through repainting and new glass and the return of ordinary things, holding their positions with a discipline the whole city could have learned from. Grief, when it is not allowed to speak, will find a shelf and stand on it.

The war ended the way a fever breaks: officially, on a date, and unofficially much more slowly, block by block, nerve by nerve. Glass came back to windows. Trams came back to the streets. Cranes stood over the city for years, and floor by floor the burnt towers grew new faces, and men in cafes argued about football again at volumes once reserved for survival. The parks that had become cemeteries stayed cemeteries, white markers in the green, and the city learned to live around them, the way tissue learns to live around what cannot be removed.

Tarik stayed. He had offers, in the years when the city’s doctors were being courted abroad, good clinics in quiet countries where it rains, and he turned them down without ever articulating why, except once, drunk on one coffee too many with an old colleague, when he came near it: the bones I know best are here. He rose the way the diligent rise. Chief resident, then consultant, then, by his fifties, the professor his students called, behind his back, with the mixed feelings of the taught, the Carpenter: exact, tireless, decent, and closed, like a well-made door.

He was, in every measurable way, a success, and knew, in the unmeasurable ways, precisely what he was. He slept with a radio murmuring so that waking would never be silent. He had married once, in the peace’s first optimism, a kind woman who spent eleven years knocking gently on the wall inside him and then, with more sorrow than anger, stopped; there were no children. He walked to work by a route that avoided one street entirely, adding four minutes, a detour so old it no longer registered as a decision. On forms requiring religion he wrote Muslim, and it was true the way a birthplace is true: where he was from, not where he lived.

His mother died in the seventeenth year of the peace, in her sleep, with the unremarkable mercy that had eluded her sons’ generation. At the funeral, a proper one this time, unhurried, in daylight, Tarik stood dry-eyed behind his professional face and heard, from among her praying friends, a sentence meant kindly that went through him like a drill: now she can look after Kenan again. Sorting her flat, he found her prayer beads wound around an old photograph of two boys over a chessboard. He took the beads home. He did not pray with them; he no longer knew how, or so he told himself. They went into his coat pocket and stayed, and his hand, in cold weather, took to finding them.

The hospital of the generator winters was long rebuilt, modernized, humming with machines that would once have seemed like sorcery. He taught in it now: trauma orthopedics for residents born after the siege, bright unbroken young people to whom that history was a subject, a thing with a syllabus. He taught them reduction and fixation, the reading of fractures, the patience of bone. He was famous among them for one strictness: he would not tolerate the word hopeless in a fracture clinic. There are non-unions, he told them. There are not hopeless bones. Bone wants to heal. Your job is to remove its excuses.

He had said that sentence for thirty years. It never once occurred to him, saying it, that he was describing anything but tibias. The mind is like that: it will let a man preach his own case to a lecture hall for decades, in perfect safety, so long as nobody names the patient.

The patient in bed six that autumn was eighty-one, a retired professor of Oriental philology with a fractured hip, a hummingbird-boned old man who had lectured on classical Arabic in this city when the library still had its million books, and who took the indignity of a broken femur as he had apparently taken everything since, with amusement. The operation, Tarik’s ten-thousandth of its kind or near it, went cleanly. On rounds afterward the old man studied the surgeon over his glasses, the way one reads a difficult manuscript, and asked, out of nowhere, whether he knew what his profession was called in the old books.

Tarik, checking the dressing, said something dry about butchery being the usual joke. The old man paid the joke no attention. Jabr, he said. The word is jabr. In the classical dictionaries it means the setting of a broken bone: the bringing of separated parts back into one line so that they knit. From it the mathematicians of old Baghdad named their new science of completing and rejoining broken quantities: al-jabr, algebra. Half the schoolchildren of the world, he said, complain about their homework in the language of your trade: the science of restoring what is broken. He settled back on the pillow, pleased, the way teachers are pleased when the world rhymes.

Then, because philologists cannot stop, he went one word further. You will find the root in a more serious place, he said, more quietly. Among the Names of Allah there is al-Jabbar. The seminaries translate it the Compeller, He whose will nothing resists, and they are right; it is a Name with mountains in it. But the first readers heard the bonesetter inside it too. Al-Jabbar: the One who sets what is broken, whose compulsion is not a tyrant’s but a surgeon’s, the force that will not leave the shattered thing shattered. The poor He enriches, the humiliated He raises, the broken He knits. The old man’s eyes had gone elsewhere, some lecture hall with its million books intact. Sixty years I taught words, he said. Most I have returned. That one I am keeping.

Tarik finished the chart and said the polite things, and went on with his rounds, and the day closed over the conversation the way water closes. Except that it did not close. The word went home with him, riding in his chest like a swallowed stone, and at eleven that night a fifty-eight-year-old professor of surgery stood in his kitchen with his grandfather’s old dictionary, kept for no reason he could have defended, looking up a word he already knew, needing to see it with his eyes. Jabr: the setting of broken bones. Jabbar: the One who sets them. On the shelf above the stove of his childhood, a knight was still deep in enemy territory. Some part of the wall in him, mortarless all these years, chose that night to move.

He did not have what people call a religious experience. He had something slower and more orthopedic. Standing in the kitchen he performed, unwillingly, the examination he had refused for thirty years, palpating the old injury like a fracture never imaged: the Tuesday, the laugh in the doorway, the one canister, the dusk light chosen so the hills would have nothing. The stranger’s forearm at eight. The whiteness. The wall. And the finding of the examination was a surgeon’s finding, precise and pitiless: non-union. The break of that spring had never knitted. He had splinted it with work and walked on it for three decades, and it had held the way such things hold, which is almost, which is until.

There are non-unions, he heard himself telling residents all those safe years. There are not hopeless bones. Your job is to remove its excuses. And underneath that, further down, arriving the way true sentences travel: what people cannot set, He can. It was, as diagnoses go, humiliating and simple. His hands had set half this city. They had never once been able to reach the fracture he carried them around on. The instrument cannot operate on itself. He had needed, his whole adult life, a Hand that was not his own, and had been too good with his own to admit it.

In his coat, on the hook by the door, were his mother’s beads. He took them out, an owner now rather than an archivist, and sat at the kitchen table, feeling entirely foolish, a grown surgeon, midnight, alone. The long formulas were gone. What remained was what she had said between the two prostrations, all those cellar winters, gone into him as sound before he was old enough to refuse it: rabbi ighfir li, warhamni, wajburni. My Lord, forgive me, and have mercy on me, and then the third word, her favourite, the word of his own trade in the mouth of a praying woman: wajburni. Set me. Mend what is broken in me.

He said it aloud in the empty kitchen, in Arabic, in his cracked unpracticed voice, once, and then for some time could say nothing at all, and it did not matter. The wall was coming down at last, and behind it, waiting with the patience of the dead, was not the horror he had feared. It was love. It was twenty litres a side. It was a boy with an unanswerable opening, laughing at the door.

He wept that night the way spring thaws a gutter, in surges, with long stillnesses between, and fell asleep at the table like a resident on call, and woke at dawn to the sound he had kept a radio murmuring thirty years to avoid, which was silence, and found it survivable. That morning he did a thing not done since boyhood, and did it badly: the ablution, the standing, the fumbled words, the forehead finally down. A surgeon spends his life bent over broken things. It had never once occurred to him that the posture was already most of a prostration. You need only stop holding the instruments, and admit whose patient you are.

What followed was not sudden light. The story would be easier and less true if it were. It was physiotherapy, the soul’s kind, slow and unglamorous, with setbacks. Prayer came back the way range of motion comes back, degree by degree, some mornings a gift and some a brick. He found a small mosque near the hospital, hid at the back among the pensioners, and discovered that the back row of a mosque is one of the great waiting rooms of the world: everyone there is in some stage of setting. He told an imam his story eventually, in pieces. The imam, a young man who had been four during the siege, listened the way good juniors assist: no sudden movements, hands ready.

On a Thursday in November he went to the corner of the park with the white markers, thirty years late, and stood before his brother’s name in the rain with his collar up, and found the visit did not break him, which is how he knew the bone had begun, at last, to knit. He told Kenan the things one tells: their mother’s peaceful end, the professor in bed six, the dictionary, the word. He said the du’a for the dead, the supplication for the dead, reading it clumsily from his phone, and did not care who saw. Walking out he passed other visitors at other markers, each in their own weather, and understood that he moved through a city of fellow patients, every one held together by Someone, most not yet knowing it.

The chessboard he resolved a year later, on Kenan’s birthday, and he did it in character, which is to say precisely. He sat down before the position out of the cupboard of his mother’s things, worked through his brother’s classified mission with an engine and an evening, and established, to his tearful satisfaction, that the unanswerable opening had in fact been unanswerable: the boy had him dead in eleven moves. He resigned formally, tipping his king to a player thirty years away, said alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah, without noticing he had said it, and put the pieces, at last, to bed in their box. Some games are not abandoned. They are adjourned, and finished in better light.

To his residents, after that year, he taught one extra thing, off the syllabus. He would hold up a healed X-ray, some old tibia with its story written around it in white, and show them the callus, the collar of new bone the body builds around a well-set break: look, the mended place is the thickest place. Done right, bone does not merely forgive the fracture, it fortifies exactly there. Then he would say, carefully, because a lecture hall holds all kinds: your hands can set a bone, but you will meet breaks your hands cannot reach, in your patients and in yourselves, and in the oldest language of this work, the One who sets those has a Name. Look it up. It rhymes with your job.

He works still, at the hour this story lets him go: an old surgeon in a rebuilt city, walking now by the shortest route, four minutes faster, past the place where the water line was, where a low stone with names on it takes two of his fingers in passing, the way other men touch doorposts. In cold weather his hand finds the beads in his pocket. In wet weather, old patients all over the city feel their long-healed fractures whisper before rain, and so does he, in the place no film ever imaged. It aches before rain. It holds. That is what setting is. The scar is healing’s handwriting, and folded inside the hardship, like a note passed in class, arrives the ease, and again, He has promised, the ease.

ayah.ar: فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا ﴿٥﴾ إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا ﴿٦﴾
ayah.en: So, indeed, with the hardship comes ease. Indeed, with the hardship comes ease.

stories.epigraph: A bone set well aches before rain, and holds.
